title: A Child Born, a Kingdom Falling
overview: Isaiah promises light and a just king from David's family for a darkened land, then turns to a grim poem about the northern kingdom of Israel collapsing under its own pride.

parts.label: Light for the north (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Zebulun and Naphtali, the lands around Galilee, were among the first territory Israel lost to Assyria, around 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). Isaiah promises that the region humbled first will be honored, its deep darkness broken by a great light.

parts.label: Joy and a broken yoke (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The joy is like harvest or victory because God has smashed the oppressor's yoke, the bar laid across a laborer's shoulders, as he once routed Midian through Gideon's small band (Judges 7). Soldiers' boots and bloodstained cloaks are burned because war gear will no longer be needed.

parts.label: A child born to rule (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: A royal child from David's family is announced who will carry the government on his shoulders, in place of the oppressor's bar in verse 4, and rule with justice and peace forever. Jewish readers often link him to King Hezekiah and read the names as praise of God, since Hebrew names are often short sentences about God, while Christians read the names, including Mighty God, as describing Jesus.

parts.label: Pride after the first blows (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Isaiah turns to the northern kingdom of Israel, here called Jacob, Ephraim and Samaria, which brushed off its losses by boasting it would rebuild with cut stone and cedar instead of mud brick and cheap sycamore fig. So God stirs up Rezin's foes (most likely Assyria), with Arameans and Philistines on either side, and a refrain begins: God's anger is not yet turned away.

parts.label: Leaders who mislead (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Because the people still do not turn back, God will cut off head and tail, palm branch and reed: the elders and dignitaries at the top and the prophets who teach lies at the bottom. In one of the book's harshest lines, the young men will find no favor, and even orphans and widows, whom God usually pities, will not be spared, because everyone is described as corrupt.

parts.label: A land eating itself (vv. 18-21)
parts.note: Wickedness spreads like wildfire from thornbushes to forest, and people tear at their own, eating 'their own offspring' or 'his own arm' as the translations differ in verse 20. Most read this as an image of civil war, with the related tribes Manasseh and Ephraim attacking each other and then Judah, which fits the string of royal murders in Israel's final years (2 Kings 15).

disagreement: Christians widely read verses 6 and 7 as about Jesus, but they differ on whether the passage first spoke of a king in Isaiah's own day, such as Hezekiah, with Jesus as its fuller meaning, or speaks of Jesus alone.
think: After a setback, how do you tell the difference between honest resilience and refusing to see what went wrong?
